# Literate Programming and the Rendered Report {#sec-literate}

::: {.bookepigraph}
```{=latex}

```
*Let us change our traditional attitude to the
construction of programs: Instead of imagining that our
main task is to instruct a computer what to do, let us
concentrate rather on explaining to human beings what we
want a computer to do.*

[Donald E. Knuth]{.smallcaps}, *Literate Programming*
(1984)

By the end of this chapter you will be able to write an
analysis whose every reported number and figure is
produced by the code sitting beside it, recognize the
handful of ways that guarantee quietly breaks, and say
precisely what a successful render does and does not
establish about an analysis's place on the
reproducibility ladder.

## Before you start

**Reading time.** About 60 minutes.

**Prerequisites.** @sec-dependencies and @sec-containers,
for the lockfile and the container, so that the seal this
chapter develops is not mistaken for either kind of pin.
@sec-levels, for the L0-L3 ladder and the
capture-versus-validation vocabulary this chapter applies
to the literate document itself. Statistically, nothing
beyond reading a scatter plot and a reported percentage is
required. R knowledge assumed: calling `library()`, writing
a short function, and reading a basic `ggplot2` call; no
prior exposure to `knitr` or Quarto chunk syntax is assumed.

**Objectives.** By the end of this chapter, can you:

- Explain Buckheit and Donoho's reproducibility argument,
  that a paper is advertising and the code and
  instructions are the scholarship, and say how a literate
  document makes the two the same artifact?
- Build a sealed render in Quarto or `knitr` and recognize
  each of the five landmines that quietly break the seal?
- Choose between HTML and PDF output, name the toolchain
  each requires, and explain why a LaTeX distribution
  belongs in the image rather than on the host?
- Explain why two renders of an unchanged document do not
  hash identically, and say what should be hashed instead?
- Place a sealed render on the L0-L3 ladder, and state
  precisely what the seal does and does not establish
  about an analysis's reproducibility?

**Outline.** Where a sealed render sits on the stack; the
oldest idea in the book, from Knuth to Buckheit and
Donoho; the R lineage from Sweave to Quarto; the sealed
render, and the same seal applied to inline numbers; the
landmines that break the seal; HTML or PDF and the
toolchain each needs; why a render will not hash the same
twice; literate programming across the archetypes; the
write-as-you-go doctrine; the cohort, continued; a worked
example; collaborating with an LLM; exercises, a cheat
sheet, and further reading.
:::

## Where this sits on the stack

A sealed render is, among this book's chapters, an unusual
case: it pins nothing new. @fig-stack-literate marks
analysis code as validated here rather than captured,
because version control already secures the code at L0;
what a sealed render adds is the check that the document's
prose and figures are actually produced by that code,
rather than pasted in and left to drift.

```{r}
#| label: fig-stack-literate
#| fig-cap: 'The determinant stack of @sec-levels, with analysis code marked as validated rather than captured. A sealed render pins no new layer of the stack; it confirms that the numbers and figures a reader sees are the ones the already-committed code actually produces, which is the capture-versus-validation distinction this chapter applies to the rendered document itself.'
#| fig-alt: !expr determinant_stack_alt(validates = c('Analysis code'))
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
plot_determinant_stack(
  validates = c('Analysis code'),
  title = 'A sealed render validates that prose and code agree; it captures nothing new')
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture or validation, for a render

A sealed render regenerates every figure and number in a
document from its own code on every build. Does sealing the
render raise a project from L0 to L1, and if not, what does
it do instead?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. Sealing the render pins no new layer of the determinant
stack: the analysis code it runs was already locatable, at
L0, because it sits in a version-controlled document.
Rather than capturing something new, the seal validates that
the document's prose agrees with that already-committed
code, by construction, every time the document is built. A
sealed, unpinned-package document and an unsealed,
fully-pinned one are both possible, which is exactly why the
seal and the ladder are different virtues.
:::
:::

## Orientation

Consider a familiar scene from a clinical-trial
analysis. The statistician has a results table in the
manuscript, produced months ago. She also has a script
that, re-run today, produces a subtly different table: a
mean that has moved in the third decimal, a confidence
interval that no longer matches the sentence that
interprets it. Neither the prose nor the code is
obviously wrong. What has failed is the correspondence
between them. The number in the paragraph was copied,
by hand, from an analysis that has since been edited,
and the paragraph was never updated. The document and
its analysis have drifted apart, silently, and no one
noticed until a reviewer asked how the interval was
computed.

This chapter is about closing that particular gap, the
gap between the prose a reader sees and the code that
produced the numbers in it. The instrument is literate
programming, by which we mean the practice of writing
the narrative and the computation in a single source
document. The figures and numbers a reader sees are then
not pasted in but regenerated every time the document is
built. We shall call a document with this property a
sealed render: prose bound to the code that produces
every number and figure it reports, so that the document
cannot silently disagree with its own analysis.

The reader will recall the ladder of reproducibility
levels that organizes this book: L0 locatable, L1
pinned packages, L2 pinned environment, L3 verified. It
is worth stating at the outset where a sealed render
sits on that ladder, because the answer is not what a
newcomer expects. A sealed render is, on its own, a
property almost orthogonal to the ladder. It guarantees
that the document agrees with the code, but it says
nothing about whether the packages are pinned, whether
the environment is fixed, or whether the outputs have
been verified. One can have a beautifully sealed
document that runs only on its author's laptop, at L0.
One can equally have a fully pinned L2 environment whose
report pastes its numbers in by hand. The seal and the
pins are different virtues, and much of the discipline
of this chapter lies in not confusing them.

That said, the sealed render is the natural home for
the machinery of the earlier chapters. It is where the
pinned packages of @sec-dependencies and the pinned
environment of @sec-containers are actually exercised,
because it is the thing that runs the code. And it is
the artifact that continuous integration renders on
every change, as we shall see in @sec-verification. The
sealed render is therefore the hinge between capturing
an environment and validating that the capture
suffices.

## The analyst's contribution

Three judgments in this chapter are the analyst's own,
and no tool makes them.

1. **Deciding what the document computes at build time
   and what it merely loads.** A figure regenerated on
   every render cannot drift from the text, which argues
   for computing everything in the document. A model
   that takes an hour to fit cannot be re-fitted on
   every render, which argues for computing it once in a
   script and caching the result. Where to draw this
   line, between the code that lives in the sealed
   document and the code that lives in
   `analysis/scripts/` with its output saved to
   `derived_data/`, is a design decision the analyst
   makes for each project, and it trades the strength of
   the seal against the cost of the render.

2. **Keeping the render sealed by refusing to reach
   outside it.** A sealed render must draw only on what
   is captured and committed. The temptations to reach
   outside are many and quiet, and we catalog them
   below as landmines: installing a package at render
   time, loading with `pacman::p_load`, reading a file
   by its absolute path on the author's machine,
   depending on state left in the session by a previous
   chunk, reading a file that was never committed. Each
   produces a document that renders perfectly for its
   author and fails for everyone else. No linter catches
   all of them; the discipline is the analyst's.

3. **Matching the claim to what the render actually
   seals.** A sealed render seals prose to code. It does
   not, by itself, seal code to its dependencies, nor
   dependencies to an environment, nor establish that
   the outputs are correct. The analyst who says 'the
   analysis is reproducible' because the report renders
   has claimed more than the seal delivers. The honest
   claim names the level actually reached, and we return
   to this below.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the analyst's third judgment

A document renders without error, and every figure in it is
produced by the code beside it. Why is 'the analysis is
reproducible' still not a claim the analyst is entitled to
make on that basis alone?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because a sealed render matches the claim to what the seal
actually delivers, which is only that the document agrees
with its own code. It says nothing about whether the
packages are pinned, the environment is fixed, or the
outputs have been shown to regenerate from a clean rebuild.
The third analyst's judgment named above, matching the
claim to what the render seals, is exactly the discipline
that stops a successful render from being overclaimed.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Literate programming.** Writing narrative prose and
  executable code together in one source document, so
  the document is at once the program and its
  explanation. The term is Knuth's.
- **Sealed render.** A document in which every reported
  number and figure is regenerated from the code that
  produces it on each build, so the prose cannot drift
  from the analysis.
- **Code chunk.** A block of executable code embedded in
  a literate document, delimited from the prose, whose
  output is inserted into the rendered document at the
  chunk's position.
- **Render (verb and noun).** To execute a literate
  source document and produce a finished output file
  (HTML, PDF, Word); and the resulting file itself.
- **Rendering toolchain.** The programs a render invokes
  behind the scenes: `knitr` or the Quarto engine to run
  the code, `pandoc` to convert the result, and, for
  PDF, a LaTeX distribution to typeset it.
- **Determinism (of a render).** The property that
  rendering the same source under the same environment
  produces a byte-for-byte identical output file. A
  rendered PDF is usually not deterministic in this
  strict sense, for reasons developed below.
- **`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`.** A conventional environment
  variable, honored by many document tools, that fixes
  the timestamp a build embeds, so that two builds do
  not differ merely because they ran at different
  moments.
- **Landmine.** A pattern in a document that makes the
  render succeed for its author and fail for a later
  reader, by reaching outside the captured and committed
  material.
:::

## The oldest idea in the book

The idea is Knuth's, and it is nearly as old as the
practice of scientific computing itself. In 1984 Knuth
proposed that a program should be written as a work of
literature, a connected narrative addressed to a human
reader, from which the machine-executable code is
extracted mechanically [@knuth1984]. He called the
practice literate programming, and inverted the usual
priority: the explanation is primary and the code is
embedded within it, rather than the code being primary
and the comments an afterthought. Knuth's own motive
was the comprehensibility of programs. The application
to reproducible research came later, and from a
different quarter.

That application, and the sentence this book takes as
its keystone, is due to Buckheit and Donoho, writing in
1995 about their WaveLab software and paraphrasing their
colleague Jon Claerbout [@buckheit1995]. Their argument,
in its clearest form, is this: an article about
computational science is not the scholarship itself, it
is merely advertising of the scholarship; the actual
scholarship is the complete software environment and
the complete set of instructions that generated the
figures. The claim is worth pausing over, because it
reframes what a paper is. On this view the printed
figures and tables are not the result but a picture of
the result, and a picture can be a faithful likeness or
a flattering one. The result itself, the thing that can
be checked and built upon, is the code and the
instructions that produce the figures. A paper that
advertises a result it cannot regenerate has, in
Claerbout's sense, advertised scholarship it does not
possess.

Literate programming is the technique that closes the
distance between the advertisement and the scholarship.
If the figure in the paper is generated, at build time,
by code that lives in the same document as the prose
around it, then the advertisement and the scholarship
are the same artifact. The figure cannot be a
flattering likeness of a result the code does not
produce, because the figure is the output of the code.
This is the whole of the reproducibility argument for
literate programming, and every practical detail in the
rest of this chapter is in service of it.

## From Sweave to Quarto

The R ecosystem has realized Knuth's idea four times
over, each realization improving on the last, and a
reader will meet all four in existing code, so it is
worth knowing the lineage.

The first was Sweave, introduced by Friedrich Leisch
around 2002 and shipped with R itself. Sweave let an
author interleave R code with LaTeX prose in a single
`.Rnw` file, ran the code, and wove the results into a
LaTeX document. It proved the concept for R and served
for a decade, but it was tied to LaTeX, awkward to
extend, and offered little control over how code and
output were formatted.

The second, and the decisive advance, was `knitr`,
written by Yihui Xie and released in 2012
[@xie2015]. `knitr` generalized Sweave in two directions
at once. It decoupled the computation from the output
format, so that the same code chunks could be woven into
LaTeX, into HTML, or into Markdown. And it gave the
author fine control over each chunk through chunk
options, the `echo`, `eval`, `warning`, and `fig.cap`
settings that recur throughout this book. `knitr` is
still the engine underneath most R literate documents,
including the executable chunk later in this chapter.

The third was R Markdown, which paired `knitr` with
`pandoc`, the universal document converter
[@xie2018]. The author now wrote in Markdown, a light and
readable prose syntax, rather than in LaTeX, and
`pandoc` converted the woven Markdown into whatever
final format was wanted: HTML for the web, PDF by way of
LaTeX, Word for a collaborator who redlines in track
changes. This is the `report.Rmd` that the zzcollab
templates scaffold, and the format in which a great deal
of current health-sciences analysis is written.

The fourth and most recent is Quarto, released by Posit
in 2022 and documented by Allaire and colleagues
[@allaire2024]. Quarto is best understood not as a
replacement for R Markdown but as its generalization
beyond R. It keeps the `knitr` engine as one option,
adds a Jupyter engine for Python and Julia, unifies the
chunk-option syntax across languages into the `#|`
comment form used in this book, and standardizes the
production of books, websites, and journal articles from
the same source. This very book is a Quarto book. For an
R analyst the migration from R Markdown to Quarto is
small, and the two will coexist for years. The important
point is that all four tools implement the same idea, and
that the idea, not the tool, is what secures the seal.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: four tools, one idea

Sweave, `knitr`, R Markdown, and Quarto differ in the
languages and output formats they support. What single
property do all four share that makes each of them, and not
merely the latest one, a literate-programming tool in
Knuth's sense?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Each interleaves narrative prose with executable code in one
source document and weaves the code's output into the
rendered result at build time, so the figure or number a
reader sees is produced by the code beside it rather than
pasted in. That property, not the particular markup
language or output format, is what secures the seal; the
four tools are successive engineerings of the same idea
Knuth proposed in 1984.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: advertisement and scholarship

Buckheit and Donoho call the published article
'advertising'. In one or two sentences, say what they
identify as the scholarship itself, and explain how a
literate document makes the advertisement and the
scholarship the same object.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The scholarship is the complete software environment and
the complete set of instructions that generated the
figures, not the printed figures themselves. A literate
document collapses the two because the figure a reader
sees is produced, at build time, by the code embedded in
the same document. The advertisement is therefore the
output of the scholarship rather than a hand-copied
picture of it, and cannot misrepresent a result the code
does not produce.
:::
:::

## The sealed render

We can now make the central idea concrete, and the
natural way to do so is to compute something. The
following chunk generates a small synthetic dataset in
the spirit of the Palmer penguins, three species
measured on two bill dimensions, fits a within-species
and a pooled relationship, and draws the result. The
point of the exercise is not the statistics, which are a
textbook instance of Simpson's paradox, but the
mechanism: this figure is produced when the book is
built, from the code the reader sees, and it cannot
therefore disagree with the sentences around it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-simpson
#| fig-cap: 'The reversal of an association upon pooling. Within each synthetic species bill depth rises with bill length (solid lines); across the pooled sample the fitted line falls (dashed). Because the figure is computed when the book is built, the described reversal cannot drift from the code that produces it.'
#| fig-alt: 'A scatter plot of bill depth against bill length for three synthetic species, each drawn in its own color. Within every species the points trend upward and carry a solid fitted line of positive slope. A single dashed line fitted to all the points pooled together is nearly flat with a slight downward tilt, the opposite sign from all three within-species lines, because the species clusters sit at descending heights as bill length increases.'
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(2024)

make_species <- function(name, mean_length, base_depth,
                         n = 60) {
  bill_length <- rnorm(n, mean = mean_length, sd = 2.2)
  bill_depth <- base_depth +
    0.15 * (bill_length - mean_length) +
    rnorm(n, sd = 0.6)
  tibble(species = name,
         bill_length = bill_length,
         bill_depth = bill_depth)
}

penguin_like <- bind_rows(
  make_species('Species A', mean_length = 39,
               base_depth = 18.5),
  make_species('Species B', mean_length = 49,
               base_depth = 18.5),
  make_species('Species C', mean_length = 47,
               base_depth = 15.0)
)

ggplot(penguin_like,
       aes(bill_length, bill_depth)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = species), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_smooth(aes(colour = species), method = 'lm',
              se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = 'lm', se = FALSE,
              colour = 'black', linetype = 'dashed') +
  labs(x = 'Bill length (mm)',
       y = 'Bill depth (mm)',
       colour = 'Species') +
  theme_minimal()
```

Within each of the three synthetic species, bill depth
rises with bill length: the three solid lines slope
upward. Pooled across the species, the relationship
reverses sign, and the dashed line comes out nearly
flat with a slight downward tilt rather than a steep
descent, because across species longer bills are
associated on average with shallower ones. The reversal
here is real but modest: it is the sign of the pooled
slope that flips, not its magnitude that grows. This is
Simpson's paradox, and it is a useful thing for a figure
to show. For our purposes,
however, the statistical lesson is secondary. The
methodological lesson is that the preceding paragraph is
safe to write. If a later edit changed the synthetic
means so that the pooled line no longer reversed, the
figure would change on the next render and the paragraph
would become visibly false, prompting its correction. In
a document that pasted the figure in as a static image,
the paragraph could go on asserting a reversal the data
no longer showed, indefinitely. The seal is precisely
this coupling: the prose and the picture rise and fall
together because they are the same computation.

Two properties of the chunk are worth naming, because
they are what keeps it sealed. First, it draws its data
from `set.seed()` and `rnorm()`, not from a file on the
author's disk, so it carries its inputs with it. Second,
it loads only packages that the build environment is
known to provide, and installs nothing. A chunk that
violated either property might still render on the
author's machine and would fail on anyone else's. The
next section is a catalog of exactly these violations.

### The seal applies to numbers in sentences, not only to figures

A figure is the conspicuous case, and the inconspicuous
one does more damage. Numbers reported in prose are
where drift is hardest to see, because a wrong number in
a sentence looks exactly like a right one.

```{r}
#| label: seal-inline
#| echo: true

d <- survival::diabetic
laser <- d[d$trt == 1, ]
n_eyes <- nrow(laser)
n_events <- sum(laser$status)
pct <- round(100 * n_events / n_eyes, 1)
```

Having computed those, the sentence that reports them
can be written with the values substituted rather than
typed. In the laser-treated arm of the retinopathy
trial there are `r n_eyes` eyes, of which `r n_events`
progressed to visual loss, a rate of `r pct` percent.

Read the source of that sentence and there are no
numerals in it. Each is an inline expression evaluated
at build time, so if the trial data were corrected, or
the arm redefined, the sentence would change with it.
This is the same seal the figure has, applied to the
unit of text where a reader is least able to detect a
lie. It is also the cheapest reproducibility discipline
in this book: it costs a few characters per number, and
it removes an entire class of error that no test, no
lockfile, and no container can reach.

The habit generalizes. Any number a reader might check
against the analysis, a sample size, a count of
exclusions, a rate, a p-value, belongs in an inline
expression. Numbers that are genuinely constants of the
study design, an enrollment target or a protocol
threshold, are properly typed, because they are inputs
rather than results.

::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## Verification

To see the seal hold on an inline number: change one line
upstream of `n_eyes`, `n_events`, or `pct` in the
`seal-inline` chunk above, say by subsetting a different
treatment arm, and rerender; the sentence that reports them
updates to match, with no edit to the prose itself. To make
it fail on purpose, replace one of the inline expressions
with the literal number it currently evaluates to, change
the upstream data, and rerender; the hardcoded sentence will
now silently disagree with the chunk that computed it,
which is the drift this chapter exists to prevent.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: which numbers are sealed

In the retinopathy example above, `n_eyes`, `n_events`, and
`pct` are each written as inline expressions. Why would it
be wrong to also write the trial's total enrollment target
of 400 eyes as an inline expression computed from the data?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Because the enrollment target is a constant of the study
design, not a result of the analysis: it was fixed by the
protocol before any data were collected, and no quantity in
the dataset determines it. Writing it as an inline
expression would make a design input masquerade as a
computed result, and would break, or silently misreport, if
the observed sample size happened to differ from the target.
Design constants are properly typed; only quantities the
analysis itself produces belong in an inline expression.
:::
:::

## The landmines that break the seal

A sealed render is fragile in a specific way: it holds
only if everything the render touches is captured and
committed. Several common patterns reach outside that
boundary, and each produces the same failure signature,
a document that renders flawlessly for its author and
errors, or worse renders differently, for a later
reader. The zzcollab publishing playbook calls these
landmines, and the name is apt, because they lie
undetonated in a document that works until the moment
someone else steps on it. We take the principal ones in
turn.

The first is **installing packages at render time**. A
chunk that calls `install.packages('somepkg')` or
`pak::pak('somepkg')` during the render reaches out to a
package repository as it builds, which makes the render
depend on network access, on the repository's state on
the day of the render, and on whatever version is
current then. The remedy is that provisioning belongs in
the environment, the Dockerfile and the lockfile of the
earlier chapters, never on the render path. A sealed
render installs nothing; it assumes its packages are
already present, pinned, and captured.

The second, a specific and common case of the first, is
**loading with `pacman::p_load`**. The `pacman` package
offers `p_load()`, which installs a package if it is
missing and then loads it, in one call. It is convenient
in interactive exploration and poisonous in a sealed
render, for two compounding reasons. It installs at
render time, with all the fragility just described; and
it defeats static dependency discovery. Tools such as
`renv` find a project's dependencies by scanning the
source for `library()`, `require()`, and `pkg::fun()`
calls; they do not parse the argument list of
`p_load(a, b, c)`, so packages loaded that way go
unrecorded in the lockfile and silently absent from the
next machine. The remedy is to replace
`pacman::p_load(a, b, c)` with explicit `library(a)`,
`library(b)`, `library(c)` calls, which both name the
dependencies for `renv` and load without installing.

The third is **absolute host paths**. A chunk that reads
`/Users/jsmith/data/cohort.csv`, or sources a LaTeX
preamble from `~/shr/preamble.tex`, embeds a fact about
one particular machine into the document. The path
exists on the author's laptop and nowhere else, so the
render fails the moment the document moves into a
container, onto a colleague's machine, or into
continuous integration. The remedy is that every file a
render touches must live inside the compendium and be
referenced by a relative path, so that the document
carries its inputs with it.

The fourth is **hidden state**. A document renders its
chunks in order, in a single R session, and it is easy to
write a chunk that depends on an object created in an
earlier chunk, or on an option set earlier, or on a
package attached earlier, without saying so. The document
renders correctly from top to bottom and fails when a
reader runs the chunk in isolation, or when a chunk is
reordered, or when caching skips the chunk that created
the state. A related anti-pattern is a chunk that calls
`rm(list = ls())` to force a clean slate. It does not
actually deliver one, since attached packages and changed
options survive it, and it can delete objects the
rendering harness itself relies on. The remedy is a
discipline of self-contained chunks and, at the level of
the toolchain, rendering each document in a fresh session
so that no state leaks in from the author's console.

The fifth is **reading uncommitted files**. A chunk may
read a file that exists in the author's working directory
but was never committed to version control, a scratch
CSV, a manually downloaded spreadsheet, an intermediate
the author produced by hand. The render succeeds for the
author, whose working tree contains the file, and fails
for anyone who clones the repository, whose working tree
does not. This is the subtlest landmine, because version
control hides it: the document and the file both sit in
the author's directory, and only a clean checkout reveals
that one of them was never tracked. The remedy is that a
sealed render reads only committed inputs, and the surest
test is to render from a fresh clone.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Pitfall

Every landmine in this section shares one signature: the
render succeeds on the author's machine. Local success is
therefore no evidence that a render is sealed. The only
convincing test is a render in a clean environment that
carries none of the author's accumulated state, which is
exactly what a container, or continuous integration,
provides. We develop that test in @sec-verification; for
now, the reader should treat 'it renders for me' as the
beginning of the question, not the end.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: diagnosing a landmine

A colleague's `report.Rmd` renders on her laptop but
fails in continuous integration with the message 'cannot
open file: data/interim.csv'. Name two distinct landmines
that could produce this symptom, and give the one-line
check that would distinguish them.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The two candidates are an absolute or author-specific
path, and an uncommitted file. They are distinguished by
inspecting version control: if `data/interim.csv` is
tracked and committed, the failure is more likely a path
problem or a working-directory assumption; if `git
status` or `git ls-files` shows the file is untracked, it
is the uncommitted-file landmine, and the file must be
committed (or the chunk that generates it must be
included in the render) before the render can seal.
Rendering from a fresh clone of the repository reproduces
the CI failure locally and settles the matter.
:::
:::

## HTML or PDF, and the toolchain each needs

A literate source document is format-agnostic; the same
`report.Rmd` can render to HTML, to PDF, or to Word. The
choice of format is not merely cosmetic, however, because
each format invokes a different toolchain behind the
render, and the environment must carry whatever the
chosen format needs.

HTML is the lighter of the two. Rendering to HTML runs
the code with `knitr` and converts the result with
`pandoc`, and both are modest, self-contained
dependencies. HTML is the natural default for a working
analysis, for a blog post, and for anything read on a
screen; it supports interactive figures, it degrades
gracefully, and it imposes the smallest environmental
burden. For most of a project's life, and for every
archetype whose output is read rather than submitted,
HTML is the sensible target.

PDF is heavier, because a PDF is typeset, and typesetting
in this ecosystem means LaTeX. Rendering to PDF runs the
same `knitr` and `pandoc` steps and then hands the result
to a LaTeX distribution, which lays out the pages,
resolves the cross-references, sets the mathematics, and
embeds the fonts. A LaTeX distribution is large, on the
order of a gigabyte for a full installation, and its
absence is the single most common cause of a PDF render
failing on a machine where the HTML render succeeds. This
is precisely the environmental problem the earlier
chapters solved, and it is why the framework's publishing
profile exists. The publishing profile builds on the
`rocker/verse` base image, which carries a base LaTeX
distribution sufficient for a straightforward render:
plain prose, ordinary tables, standard mathematics. It
does not carry a full LaTeX distribution, so a document
that reaches for a package the base omits, dense tables,
`moderncv`-style layouts, and similar, still needs that
package installed with `tlmgr` before it will render.
zzcollab's own publishing profile pre-installs roughly two
dozen such packages at image build time precisely because
the base image does not ship them. A project that renders
to PDF chooses the publishing profile at initialization;
a project that renders only to HTML does not need it, and
pays neither the build time nor the image size that the
LaTeX toolchain costs. The playbook that migrates a
compendium to the publishing profile turns on exactly this
question: it scans every report's YAML for a
`pdf_document` or `latex_engine` output and, finding one,
concludes that the verse base is required.

The general principle is the one that runs through the
whole book. The literate document declares what it wants
to be, and the environment must be provisioned to supply
it. HTML asks little; PDF asks for LaTeX; and the honest
way to supply LaTeX is to pin it in the image, not to
install it, fragilely and at render time, on whatever
machine happens to build the document.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: choosing the profile

A project renders only to HTML today, but a collaborator
wants to add a `pdf_document2` output to one report next
month. What, if anything, should change about the project's
Docker image now, and why might waiting be the wrong call?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Nothing needs to change now; an HTML-only project does not
need the publishing profile's LaTeX distribution and should
not pay its build time or image size before it is needed.
What matters is recognizing, once the PDF output is added,
that the project must move to the publishing profile (built
on `rocker/verse`) and confirm any package-specific LaTeX
dependencies are present, rather than installing `tlmgr`
packages ad hoc on whichever machine first attempts the PDF
render. Waiting to decide is fine; waiting to act once the
YAML declares `pdf_document2` reintroduces exactly the
render-time, machine-specific fragility this chapter warns
against.
:::
:::

## Why a rendered document will not hash the same twice

We come now to a subtlety that surprises many analysts
and that shapes how verification is done in
@sec-verification. It is natural to suppose that the way
to check a reproducible report is to render it twice and
compare the two output files: if the analysis is
reproducible, surely the PDFs should be identical? They
will not be, and the reason is instructive.

A rendered PDF, and to a lesser degree a rendered HTML
file, embeds metadata that has nothing to do with the
analysis and everything to do with the moment of the
render. A PDF carries a creation timestamp and a
modification timestamp in its metadata; it carries an
internal document identifier, often randomly generated;
and when it subsets the fonts it uses, it assigns those
subsets internal names that can vary between builds. Two
renders of byte-for-byte identical source, in the same
environment, minutes apart, therefore produce two PDF
files that differ in their bytes, even though every
number and figure in them is identical. The difference is
real at the level of the file and spurious at the level
of the science.

Part of this non-determinism can be normalized away. Many
document tools, including LaTeX and `pandoc`, honor a
conventional environment variable, `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`,
which fixes the timestamp the build embeds to a specified
value rather than reading the wall clock. Setting it
removes the timestamp difference, and a determined
practitioner can normalize further, stripping identifiers
and canonicalizing font-subset names, until two renders
do hash alike. This is worthwhile work in some settings,
notably in the reproducible-builds movement for operating
systems. For a research compendium it is usually effort
misplaced, because it fights the symptom rather than
addressing the target.

The resolution the framework adopts is to hash the right
thing. Verification, developed in @sec-verification, does
not hash the rendered document. It hashes the
computational outputs, the derived datasets, the model
objects, the figure data, the numbers themselves, which
are deterministic under a fixed environment and a fixed
seed in a way the typeset PDF is not. The rendered report
is a human-facing artifact, a faithful presentation of
those outputs, and it is checked by regenerating it and
confirming that the outputs it presents match the
recorded baseline, not by demanding that its bytes be
identical. It is worth noting that the framework goes
further in the opposite direction for provenance: its
render hook deliberately stamps each rendered PDF with the
render time and the git version of the source, in a
footer, precisely so that a reader can tell two renders
apart and trace each to its source commit. The rendered
document is thus treated as a dated, signed presentation
of a result, not as the hashable object of record. The
object of record is the computation.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

This chapter's own executed chunks, `fig-simpson`, the
inline-sealed retinopathy sentence, and the cohort passage
below, are sealed, every number in them regenerates from
the code beside it, but that seal alone leaves them at no
higher than L0, since nothing in this chapter pins the
packages or the environment that produced them.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: two PDFs, one analysis

Two renders of the same, unchanged `report.Rmd` produce PDF
files with different checksums. Does this mean the analysis
is not reproducible?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The checksums differ because of metadata that has
nothing to do with the analysis, a creation timestamp, a
document identifier, font-subset names, not because the
figures or numbers changed. The right question is whether
the computational outputs, the numbers and figures the
document presents, regenerate within a stated tolerance, and
that is answered by hashing the outputs themselves, not the
typeset file. A rendered document's bytes are not the object
of record; the computation is.
:::
:::

## Literate programming across the archetypes

The weight the sealed render carries varies sharply across
the five archetypes; @tbl-archetype-weight in
@sec-compendium is the reference. It is center of gravity
for the manuscript, multiplied across many posts for the
blog, and lighter for an internal data-analysis summary.
The two cases most worth stating here are the ones a reader
fixed on the manuscript will misjudge. The **R-package**
archetype has no sealed report at all: its 'document' is
its help pages and vignettes, generated from roxygen
comments and demonstrating the package rather than
reporting an analysis, and its correctness rests on the
tests of @sec-testing, not on a rendered result. The
**simulation-study** archetype inverts the usual weight for
a different reason: the heavy computation, hours or days of
Monte Carlo replicates, cannot live in the sealed document,
so it runs once in `analysis/scripts/`, seeded with the care
@sec-levels stressed, and saves its results to
`derived_data/`; the literate report then becomes a thin
presentation layer that loads and presents those results
rather than recomputing them on each build. In every case
the underlying machinery, `knitr` or Quarto, chunks,
committed inputs, a pinned environment, is the same; only
how heavily an archetype leans on it changes.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: the package that renders nothing

An R package maintainer is told, by a colleague who has read
only the manuscript archetype's section above, that the
package needs a `report.Rmd` to be reproducible. Is the
colleague right?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No. The R-package archetype has no single analysis to
report, so it has no `report.Rmd` to seal; its literate
surface is the vignette and the roxygen-generated help page,
and its correctness is established by `R CMD check` and the
test suite rather than by a rendered result. Demanding a
manuscript-style sealed report of a package applies this
chapter's heaviest-weight case to the one archetype where
the machinery is largely absent.
:::
:::

## The write-as-you-go doctrine

There remains a matter of practice rather than mechanism,
and it is the one on which experienced compendium authors
are most insistent. The traditional order of work runs:
write the analysis scripts, generate the results, then
start the manuscript, and finally copy the results into
the prose. This order builds the drift we opened the
chapter with directly into the workflow, because the
copying is manual and the results and the prose are
separate artifacts from the start.

The write-as-you-go doctrine inverts the order. One
creates the `report.Rmd` on the first day of the project,
before there is any analysis to report. Into it one
writes the research question, the background, and the
planned methods as prose. The analysis code is then added
inline, in chunks, as the work proceeds, so that from the
first day the numbers in the document are computed rather
than copied. As patterns emerge, code that is used more
than once is extracted from the document into a function
in `R/`, and as those functions stabilize they acquire
tests in `inst/tinytest/`, the subject of @sec-testing.
When a computation grows too slow to run on every render,
it moves to `analysis/scripts/`, is run once, and saves
its result for the document to load. This is the
build-time-versus-load-time boundary named among the
analyst's contributions above. The compendium's directory
structure, in this view, emerges from the writing rather
than preceding it: the manuscript drives the analysis,
and the `R/`, `tests/`, and `scripts/` directories fill
in as the code in the document matures.

The doctrine is not merely tidy. Its reproducibility
payoff is that the document is sealed from the first day
and stays sealed, because there is never a phase in which
results live in the prose by having been copied there.
The number in the paragraph was computed by the chunk
above it on the very first render, and on every render
since. The drift that opened this chapter has no moment
at which to enter.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: why day one, not day thirty

The write-as-you-go doctrine creates `report.Rmd` before any
analysis exists. What specifically would be lost by instead
writing the analysis scripts first for a month and only then
starting the document, even if every number in the eventual
document were still computed rather than typed?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

Nothing would be lost about any individual number's seal, if
the author were careful. What would be lost is the absence
of a phase in which copying could occur: a month of
scripts-first work creates thirty days during which a
results-in-progress tempts an author to paste a number into
a slide or an email, and the habit of pasting is exactly
what later infects the manuscript once it starts. Starting
the document on day one removes the opportunity for that
habit to form, rather than merely disciplining the author
once it already has.
:::
:::

## Worked example

Let us assemble the pieces into a concrete `report.Rmd`,
as a health scientist beginning a cohort analysis would.
On the first day, before any data are analyzed, the author
creates the report and writes its header. A representative
YAML header, shown here as a static block rather than
rendered, declares the title, the authorship, the output
formats, and the bibliography:

```yaml
---
title: 'Bill morphology across three penguin species'
author:
  - name: A. Analyst
    affiliation: Department of Epidemiology
date: '`r format(Sys.Date(), "%B %d, %Y")`'
output:
  bookdown::pdf_document2:
    number_sections: true
    keep_tex: true
  bookdown::html_document2:
    toc: true
bibliography: references.bib
---
```

Two features of this header repay attention. The `output`
field names two formats, a PDF built through LaTeX for
submission and an HTML version for reading on a screen. The
project that renders the former needs the publishing
profile and its baked-in LaTeX distribution, while the
latter needs neither. The `date` field is itself a small
literate device: rather than a fixed string, it holds an
inline R expression that inserts the render date, so the
header cannot claim a date the render did not have. The
provenance footer discussed below is not declared in this
header at all; it is applied by the render tooling
(`make docker-render`, by way of `tools/stamp-render.R`)
rather than by the YAML.

Below the header the author writes a setup chunk that fixes
the chunk defaults and loads the packages the document
uses, naming each with an explicit `library()` call so that
`renv` can discover them and no package is installed at
render time:

```r
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  warning = FALSE,
  fig.path = '../figures/'
)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

From here the write-as-you-go doctrine takes over. The
author writes the introduction as prose, adds a
data-summary chunk, then the modeling chunk that produces
the analysis, then the figure, exactly the sealed
`fig-simpson` chunk demonstrated earlier in this chapter,
which computes its result at build time and carries its
synthetic inputs with it. Each number the introduction and
discussion cite is inserted by an inline expression that
reads the computed object, never typed by hand. Rendering
the document inside the container, with `make docker-render`
or its equivalent, executes every chunk in a fresh session,
regenerates every figure, and produces the PDF and HTML,
each carrying the render's provenance footer.

The result is a document that is sealed by construction. To
convince oneself that the seal holds, and does not merely
appear to hold on the author's machine, one renders it from
a fresh clone of the repository inside the pinned
environment (habit 6). If it renders there, with no file
missing and no package installed on the fly, the seal is
real. If it fails, one of the landmines catalogued above has
been stepped on, and the failure names which.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the header's `date` field buys

The YAML header above sets the `date` field to an inline
expression that evaluates `Sys.Date()` at render time,
rather than a fixed string typed on the day the project
began. What would be lost by typing the date literally
instead, and is this an instance of the same seal as the
figure and the inline numbers?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

A literal date would freeze at whatever day it was typed,
so a document rendered months later would still carry its
first day's date, silently misrepresenting when the reader's
copy was actually produced. It is the same seal, applied to
metadata rather than to a result: the date is computed from
the render itself rather than pasted in, so it cannot drift
from the moment it claims to describe.
:::
:::

## The cohort, continued

The same discipline applies directly to this book's own
running cohort. The chunk below loads and cleans the extract
and computes two numbers the way every sealed document
should, as objects a sentence can cite rather than as values
copied from a console.

```{r}
cohort <- clean_cohort(load_cohort(
  '../data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'))
n_cohort <- nrow(cohort)
pct_missing_outcome <- round(
  100 * mean(is.na(cohort$incident_dm)), 1)
```

The cleaned cohort holds `r n_cohort` records, of which
`r pct_missing_outcome` percent carry no recorded outcome.
Both numbers are inline expressions reading `cohort`, not
literals typed after a console check, so a later edit to
`clean_cohort()`, or to the raw extract, changes this
paragraph on the next render rather than leaving it to drift
the way the orientation's opening story describes. Nothing
about this passage pins a package or an environment; it is
the seal, and only the seal, demonstrated on the book's own
data rather than on a hypothetical one.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what the cohort passage does and does not show

The chunk above reports that `r pct_missing_outcome` percent
of the cleaned cohort is missing an outcome. Does rerunning
this chunk on a colleague's machine, and getting the
identical number, tell that colleague anything about whether
the number is correct?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

No, for the same reason @sec-testing presses at length. An
identical rerun shows that the document's prose agrees with
its own code and that the code is at least stable across
the two machines on the one layer this chapter touches; it
does not show that `clean_cohort()`'s missingness
calculation is the one the analyst intended. That
correctness question belongs to a unit or data-validation
test with an independent oracle, not to the seal, which
confirms agreement between prose and code and nothing about
whether the code is right.
:::
:::

## Collaborating with an LLM

A language model is a capable assistant for literate
documents, and a treacherous one, because its fluency in
producing chunks that run on the author's machine is
exactly the fluency that plants landmines. Three exchanges
illustrate the pattern of use and the verification the
analyst must supply.

::: {.callout-important}
## Restricted data

A literate document mixes code with data and results, so it
is easy to paste too much (habit 3). Never paste or upload
protected health information, identifiable or
agreement-restricted data, or outputs derived from them (a
rendered table of small cells included), into a model unless
the endpoint is approved by the reader's institution for
that data; describe the structure instead, with column
names, types, and a synthetic example. A coding agent asked
to render the document reads the data it renders, so it
belongs only in projects whose data it is allowed to see.
:::

**Prompt.** 'Write a `knitr` chunk that loads `dplyr` and
`survival` and reads the CSV at
`analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv`, which has columns
`mrn` (character), `enroll_date` (character, in two date
formats), `hba1c` and `bmi` (numeric), and `incident_dm`
(integer, 0 or 1, with missing values).'

*Watch for.* A model will often reach for convenience over
seal. It may emit `pacman::p_load(...)`, or an
`install.packages()` call, or a `library(pacman)` line,
because these are common in the training data; and it may
read the data from an absolute path it invents, such as
`/Users/you/data/cohort.csv`, or from a path outside the
project.

*Verification.* Insist on explicit `library()` calls, one
per package, with no installation on the render path, and a
relative path to a committed file under the compendium.
Then apply the decisive test: render the chunk from a fresh
clone inside the container. A chunk that survives that test
is sealed; a chunk that only ran in the author's console is
not, whatever the model asserted.

**Prompt.** 'My PDF render fails with a LaTeX error but the
HTML render works. Fix it.'

*Watch for.* A model may propose to install a LaTeX package
at render time, or to add a `tinytex::tlmgr_install()` call
inside a chunk, which converts an environment problem into
a render-time landmine and makes the document depend on
network access and repository state.

*Verification.* The correct locus of the fix is the
environment, not the document. Confirm that the failure is
a missing LaTeX toolchain, and provision it by building on
the publishing profile so that LaTeX is baked into the
image, rather than installing it as the document renders.
Verify that the PDF then renders in the container with
nothing installed on the fly.

**Prompt.** 'Check that this analysis is reproducible.'

*Watch for.* A model will frequently equate a successful
render with reproducibility, and report the analysis as
reproducible on the strength of the document having built.
This conflates the seal with the level, the confusion this
chapter exists to prevent.

*Verification.* Ask, and answer, the level question
explicitly. A render that succeeds demonstrates the seal.
Whether the analysis is pinned (L1), environment-fixed
(L2), or verified (L3) is a separate question, settled by
the lockfile, the container, and a baseline test run after
a clean rebuild (@sec-levels), not by the fact of a render. State
the level actually reached and no more.

The same disclosure obligation applies to a literate
document. If a language model drafted or edited a chunk, a
caption, or a paragraph of prose here, that use belongs in
the manuscript's methods section or acknowledgments, not
left unstated. Current editorial guidance, including from
the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors,
treats AI assistance as disclosable, not authorable: a
model cannot be listed as an author, because it cannot take
responsibility for the work, but silence about its use is
not an option either. Record which model, or model family
and version, helped produce the document, and roughly when,
exactly as the compendium already records an R and package
version in its lockfile. A render's seal attests that the
code ran and the prose agrees with it; it says nothing
about whether a sentence of prose, or a chunk of code, was
drafted by a person or a model, so that provenance has to
be recorded separately, in prose the seal does not cover.
This record matters because a model is not a versioned,
reproducible dependency the way a package is. The same
model name can behave differently across releases, a
provider can retire or silently update a model identifier
the document depended on, and even one unchanged version is
not guaranteed to produce identical text or code from one
call to the next. 'Drafted with language-model assistance,
a general-purpose model, approximately mid-2026' is a
usable record for a future reader auditing the document;
'AI-assisted' alone is not, any more than 'used some R
packages' would be an acceptable substitute for a lockfile
entry.

## Exercises

1. Take an existing `.Rmd` or `.qmd` document of your own
   in which at least one reported number was typed into the
   prose by hand. Replace that number with an inline R
   expression that computes it from the data, render the
   document, and confirm the value is unchanged. Then edit
   the data slightly, re-render, and observe the number
   update in the prose. Describe what would have happened to
   the hand-typed number under the same edit.

2. Write a short `knitr` or Quarto chunk that generates
   synthetic data with `set.seed()` and produces a figure,
   as the `fig-simpson` chunk in this chapter does. Render
   it twice and confirm the figure is identical. Then remove
   the `set.seed()` call, render twice more, and explain in
   terms of this chapter why the figure now differs between
   renders and what that implies for the seal.

3. Deliberately plant each of the five landmines from this
   chapter, one at a time, in a copy of a working document:
   an `install.packages()` call, a `pacman::p_load()` call,
   an absolute host path, a chunk that depends on hidden
   state from an earlier chunk, and a read of an uncommitted
   file. For each, predict whether the document will still
   render on your own machine, then test the prediction by
   rendering from a fresh clone in a clean environment.

4. Locate a document in your work that renders to PDF, and
   determine whether the LaTeX toolchain it requires is
   pinned in an environment or assumed present on the host.
   If it is assumed present, describe the steps by which you
   would move it into the publishing profile, and state
   which reproducibility level the move would raise the
   project to.

5. Render a PDF from a literate document twice, minutes
   apart, and compare the two files byte for byte (for
   instance with a checksum). Confirm that they differ,
   inspect the metadata to identify what differs, and
   explain why hashing the rendered document would be the
   wrong basis for verification. Then describe what should
   be hashed instead.

6. For each of the five archetypes named in this chapter,
   the manuscript, the blog, the data analysis, the R
   package, and the simulation study, write one or two
   sentences stating what the literate document renders in
   that archetype, if anything, and how heavily the
   reproducibility weight rests on the render as opposed to
   elsewhere.

7. On the running cohort compendium, run
   `clean_cohort(load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'))`
   and write a one-sentence, inline-sealed report of the
   cleaned row count and the percentage of rows missing an
   outcome, in the style of 'The cohort, continued' above.
   Report the two specific numbers a grading script could
   check without rendering anything: `nrow(cohort)` and the
   percentage missing `incident_dm`, rounded to one decimal
   place.

8. This exercise returns to the dependency-pinning
   discipline of Chapter 6 (@sec-dependencies). The
   `fig-simpson` chunk in this chapter loads `dplyr`,
   `tibble`, and `ggplot2` with explicit `library()` calls.
   Run `renv::dependencies()` on this chapter's own `.qmd`
   file, as @sec-dependencies's own cohort exercise runs it
   on `R/cohort.R`, and report which of those three packages
   the scan finds referenced. Then explain why a chunk that
   instead called `pacman::p_load(dplyr, tibble, ggplot2)`
   would pass this chapter's own render yet be invisible to
   that scan, tying the two chapters' landmines together.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Most of
this chapter's exercises are performed on a document of the
reader's own, so their outputs vary; the boxes record what
should happen and why.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

The substitution replaces a literal with an expression, so
that a sentence reading 'The mean age was 61.4 years'
becomes, in the source,
`r knitr::inline_expr('round(mean(cohort$age), 1)')`
written inline where the number used to be.

On the first render the printed value is unchanged,
which is the confirmation that the expression computes
what the hand-typed number claimed. After a small edit to
the data, the prose updates on re-render.

**What would have happened to the hand-typed number.**
Nothing at all. It would have sat in the paragraph,
unchanged and now wrong, with no error raised anywhere and
nothing in the document to indicate a problem. That
silence is the whole difficulty: the failure produces no
symptom, so it is found only when someone independently
recomputes the number, which for most published analyses
is never.

This is the drift the chapter opens with, in its smallest
form. The inline expression does not make the number
correct; it makes the number *bound*, so that it cannot
disagree with the analysis without the disagreement being
visible on the next render.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

With `set.seed()` present, the two renders produce
identical figures, because the synthetic data is a
deterministic function of the seed and the code.

With the call removed, the generator is initialized from
varying session state, so each render draws a different
sample and the figure differs between renders.

**Why this matters for the seal, and what the seal is
not.** The seal binds prose to code: it guarantees that
the figure a reader sees was produced by the code shown
beside it. That guarantee still holds without the seed.
What fails is something adjacent and easily confused with
it, which is that the document is no longer a
deterministic function of its source. Two people rendering
the same committed document get different figures, so any
sentence in the prose describing the figure, 'the
association reverses within each group', 'three points lie
outside the interval', can become false without the code
changing.

The precise statement is that a seal makes the document
agree with its code, and a seed makes the code agree with
itself across runs. An unseeded literate document is
sealed and not reproducible, which is a good illustration
of the chapter's warning that the seal and the pins are
different virtues.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

The predictions worth making before testing, and what
actually happens.

**`install.packages()`.** Renders on your machine, and
probably on the fresh clone too, since it installs what it
needs. That is what makes it insidious: it does not fail,
it silently installs whatever version is current, so the
document renders against a different package set than the
one it was written for. The landmine here is not a broken
render but an unpinned one.

**`pacman::p_load()`.** The same, with an additional
failure mode: it installs `pacman` itself if absent, so
the document reaches out to the network on a machine where
nothing was declared.

**An absolute host path.** Renders on your machine and
fails immediately on the fresh clone, with a
'cannot open file' error. This is the friendliest landmine,
because it announces itself.

**A chunk depending on hidden state from an earlier
chunk.** Usually renders in both places, since a full
render executes chunks in order in one session. It fails
when someone runs the chunk in isolation, or when the
chunk order changes, or when caching or `freeze` skips the
chunk that established the state. Intermittent and hard to
diagnose.

**A read of an uncommitted file.** Renders on your machine
and fails on the fresh clone, the same symptom as the
absolute path, which is exactly why the chapter pairs them
and asks for a distinguishing check: inspect version
control to see whether the file is tracked.

The general lesson from the prediction exercise: two of
the five fail loudly, and the three that render anyway are
the dangerous ones. Rendering from a fresh clone catches
the loud two reliably and the quiet three only sometimes,
which is the argument for continuous integration in
@sec-verification.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

No single correct answer, since it depends on the
document. The determination is usually quick: if the
project contains no Dockerfile and no environment
specification naming a TeX distribution, the toolchain is
assumed present on the host, which is the common case.

**The steps to move it in.** Select the publishing profile,
so the base image becomes `rocker/verse`, which carries the
LaTeX toolchain. Pin that base by digest. Confirm that the
document's specific LaTeX dependencies are present, since
`verse` carries a substantial but not unlimited TeX
installation, and add any missing packages explicitly to
the Dockerfile rather than letting a run-time installer
fetch them. Then render inside the container and confirm
the PDF is produced.

**Which level the move raises the project to.** L2, from
wherever it was before, provided a lockfile is also in
place. The precise claim is worth stating carefully,
because the exercise invites an overclaim: moving the
toolchain into the image is the L1-to-L2 step for the
*rendering* dependency specifically. If the packages were
never pinned, the project moves to L2 only once the
lockfile is restored inside the image too, since L2
presupposes L1. And it does not reach L3, because no
baseline test has yet shown that the render regenerates its
recorded outputs within a stated tolerance.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

The two PDFs differ, and their checksums differ.

**What differs.** Inspecting the metadata, with
`pdfinfo` or by examining the raw file, shows a
`CreationDate` and a `ModDate` recording the moment of the
render. Depending on the engine, the file may also embed a
document identifier derived from the time, font subset
tags that vary with the subsetting order, and absolute
paths from the build directory. None of this is the
analysis; all of it changes between renders.

**Why hashing the rendered document is the wrong basis for
verification.** The check would fail on every rebuild,
including rebuilds in which nothing whatever changed. A
check that always fails carries no information, and its
practical effect is worse than no check at all, because it
trains whoever sees it to ignore the failure. A
verification gate is useful in proportion to how reliably
its failures mean something.

**What should be hashed instead.** The deterministic
computational outputs that feed the report: the derived
datasets, the fitted model objects, the results tables.
Each of these changes its checksum exactly when a number
changes, and not otherwise, so a failure is informative.
The render gate then sits alongside as a separate check
confirming that the document still builds from those
outputs.

It is worth noting that byte-identical PDFs are
attainable, by setting `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` and freezing
font subsetting, and that this is a fragile route to a
result the output hashes give directly. The chapter's
position is that one should hash what is deterministic
rather than work to make the non-deterministic thing
deterministic.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**Manuscript.** The literate document renders the paper
itself, and the reproducibility weight rests almost
entirely on the render: the deliverable *is* the rendered
artifact, and every number in it must be computed rather
than typed. This is the archetype the machinery was
designed for.

**Blog.** Renders each post. The weight is substantial but
lighter than the manuscript's, because the stakes of a
drifted number are lower and posts are usually
self-contained. The distinctive pressure is longevity:
posts are written once and read for years, so the pinned
packages matter more than the render does.

**Data analysis.** Renders a report, if there is one, and
the weight is moderate. Much of the analysis lives in
scripts producing derived data, and the report summarizes
rather than performs. The seal matters for the summary;
the reproducibility of the analysis rests mainly on the
scripts and the pinned environment.

**R package.** Renders nothing, or at most a vignette. The
weight rests almost entirely elsewhere, on `R CMD check`
and the unit tests, which bind behavior to claims more
strongly than prose can. A vignette that renders is a
convenience and a demonstration rather than the
deliverable.

**Simulation study.** Renders a report on the results, if
one exists. The weight rests overwhelmingly on the seed
and the generator rather than on the render: a sealed
document reporting an unseeded simulation is bound to its
code and still not reproducible, as exercise 2 shows.

The pattern across the five is that the render carries the
most weight exactly where the document is the deliverable,
and that in the two archetypes where it carries least, the
package and the simulation, a different mechanism, tests
and seeds respectively, does the binding instead.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 7

```r
cohort <- clean_cohort(
  load_cohort('analysis/data/raw_data/cohort_raw.csv'))
n_cohort <- nrow(cohort)
pct_missing <- round(100 * mean(is.na(cohort$incident_dm)), 1)
```

The sealed sentence reads: 'The cleaned cohort holds
`r knitr::inline_expr('n_cohort')` records, of which
`r knitr::inline_expr('pct_missing')` percent carry no
recorded outcome', with both values inserted as inline
expressions rather than typed after a console check.

**The two numbers**, run against the extract as committed:
the cleaned cohort holds 337 rows, and 9.5 percent of them
are missing `incident_dm`. These are exactly the values
`nrow(cohort)` and
`round(100 * mean(is.na(cohort$incident_dm)), 1)` return, so
a grading script can check them without rendering the
document at all. A reader who gets different numbers has
either an edited extract or a different `clean_cohort()`
than the one this book ships, which is itself a useful
diagnostic, as the parallel exercise in @sec-testing notes
for the same two functions.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 8

```r
renv::dependencies('analysis/report/07-literate-programming.qmd')
```

The scan finds `dplyr`, `tibble`, and `ggplot2` all
referenced, among other packages this chapter's prose and
worked example load or name (`knitr`, `rmarkdown`,
`pkgload`, and, from the `tbl-diabetic-arms`-style examples
elsewhere in the book, `survival`). All three of the
`fig-simpson` chunk's explicit `library()` calls are
therefore visible to the scan and would be pinned by
`renv::snapshot()` and checked by `make check-renv`.

**Why `pacman::p_load()` would be invisible to it.**
`renv::dependencies()` finds packages by recognizing the
syntactic forms `library(pkg)`, `require(pkg)`, and
`pkg::fun()`, the same forms @sec-dependencies's
dependency-triad check looks for. A call to
`pacman::p_load(dplyr, tibble, ggplot2)` recognizes `pacman`
itself, because that is a namespaced call, but the three
packages named as bare arguments inside it are not calls of
any of those three recognized forms, so the scan does not
see them. The chunk would still run, and would still render,
on a machine where those packages happened to be installed,
which is exactly this chapter's warning about
`pacman::p_load()`: it reaches outside the committed
lockfile at render time, and @sec-dependencies's own gate,
built on the same kind of syntactic scan as
`renv::dependencies()`, cannot catch what it cannot see
either. The two chapters' landmines are the same landmine,
met twice: once as a render-time install, once as an
invisible, unpinned dependency.
:::

## Cheat sheet

| Command or rule | What it does |
|---|---|
| `library(pkg)`, one per package | Names a dependency explicitly so `renv` can find it; never `pacman::p_load()`. |
| An inline R expression in prose | Seals a number in prose to the code that computes it (habit 2). |
| `knitr::opts_chunk$set(...)` | Sets chunk defaults, `echo`, `message`, `warning`, `fig.path`, once near the top. |
| `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` | Fixes the embedded build timestamp, so two renders agree on that one field. |
| `make docker-render` | Renders inside the pinned container and stamps the provenance footer (habit 6). |
| Five landmines | Installing at render time; `pacman::p_load()`; an absolute host path; hidden cross-chunk state; reading an uncommitted file. |
| Rule of thumb | A sealed render binds prose to code; it pins no package, no environment, and proves nothing correct. |
| Rule of thumb | Hash the computational outputs, not the rendered PDF or HTML; the render's bytes are not the object of record. |
| Habit 6 | Rebuild from clean, on a machine that is not yours, to test whether the seal actually holds. |
| Habit 7 | Write the honest level down; 'it renders' is a claim about the seal, not about L1, L2, or L3. |

## Further reading

The foundational statement of literate programming is
@knuth1984, which repays reading in the original for its
inversion of the usual priority of code over explanation,
even though its concrete apparatus is now of historical
interest. The reproducibility argument this chapter takes
as its keystone is @buckheit1995, whose paraphrase of
Claerbout, that the article is advertising and the code and
instructions are the scholarship, is the single most cited
sentence in this literature and the one worth committing to
memory. The earlier formulation in @claerbout1992 and the
signal-processing lineage surveyed by @vandewalle2009 give
the argument its original setting.

On the R realizations, @xie2015 is the definitive treatment
of `knitr` by its author, and @xie2018 documents R Markdown
and its `pandoc`-based toolchain; @allaire2024 introduces
Quarto and is the natural starting point for a reader
beginning today. The compendium framing that binds the
literate document to the rest of the project is
@gentleman2007, who first proposed the compendium as an
executable document, and @marwick2018, whose `rrtools`
operationalizes it around a `report.Rmd`. For the practical
habits, @sandve2013 and @wilson2017 both stress recording
exactly how each figure was produced, which is the sealed
render stated as a rule of conduct. The determinism
questions touched on here connect to the verification
machinery of @sec-verification and, in the wider setting of
reproducible builds, to a substantial body of systems
literature that a reader pursuing byte-level reproduction of
documents will want to consult beyond the scope of this
book.
